claims.text: The extent of Q235 hot-corrosion degradation or protection at 700–900 °C is controlled by its intrinsic grain structure.
A finer grain structure has a higher density of grain boundaries.
Higher grain-boundary density promotes rapid and uniform nucleation of an adherent iron-oxide scale.
A uniform, adherent iron-oxide scale temporarily slows further corrosive attack.
Coarse grains cause heterogeneous oxide growth and scale discontinuities.
Scale discontinuity or spallation exposes fresh metal and accelerates material loss.
As-received Q235 has an inherent ferritic microstructure.
The grain size of as-received Q235 can vary with processing history.
Annealing treatments can produce controlled fine, medium, and coarse grain structures in Q235.
The proposed grain-size mechanism applies in 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salt at 700–900 °C.
Formation and integrity of a protective oxide scale are the primary governing factors under the proposed exposure conditions.
The proposed mechanism does not extend to room-temperature atmospheric corrosion.
Additional alloying elements can alter molten-salt surface reactions and may invalidate extrapolation of the grain-size mechanism.
High chromium levels can produce inherently protective oxide films.
Fine-grained samples will develop more coherent and adherent oxide scales than coarse-grained samples.
Fine-grained samples will show lower mass change or weight loss than coarse-grained samples.
As-received Q235 has an intermediate grain size and will exhibit corrosion behavior between the fine- and coarse-grained conditions.
Oxide-growth kinetics may vary across the 700–900 °C range.
A lack of statistically significant grain-size-dependent differences in scale uniformity, adherence, and mass change would reject the proposed grain-boundary-mediated mechanism.
